idiom_name: abstract base entity + @Entity per concrete class
implementation_notes: TypeORM documents this pattern by name: define an abstract base class carrying the shared @Column/@PrimaryGeneratedColumn members and extend it in each @Entity, and 'all columns (relations, embeds, etc.) from parent entities will be inherited and created in final entities' - three entities yield three tables and no table for the base. Do not decorate the base class (and do not reach for @TableInheritance/@ChildEntity, which is single table inheritance), and remember that legacy decorators plus reflect-metadata are required, which is why this variant declares a decorator feature requirement. Choose it when the application already runs TypeORM and most reads target one concrete repository.
pitfalls: TypeORM's inheritance is compile-time: the base class contributes columns to each table, so changing a base column means a migration per table and there is no runtime link between them.
Decorating the base class with @Entity (or adding @TableInheritance) creates a table or a discriminator and switches the mapping to single table inheritance.
Mixed queries need one repository per concrete entity or a raw UNION ALL - there is no polymorphic repository - and per-table generated ids are not unique across the hierarchy.

variants.name: Prisma per-table models (no inheritance mapping)
variants.idiom_name: one Prisma model per concrete table + raw UNION ALL for mixed reads
variants.implementation_notes: Prisma has no inheritance: 'on a relational database, a model becomes a table', so each concrete class becomes its own model with the shared columns repeated, and a mixed list is either several ORM-client reads or one raw SQL statement (db.raw.sql) with NULL padding and a literal type tag. Nothing generates the duplicated columns or the union, so this is the manual route - the right one when the team prefers a schema-first toolchain over decorator-based entities. Knex gives the same shape one level lower with a query builder per table.
pitfalls: Prisma models share no base definition, so the duplicated columns must be kept in sync by hand (or generated) and no migration ties them together.
Referential integrity to 'any subclass' is impossible: a relation must point at one model's table, so polymorphic references need a registry table.
Per-model auto-increment ids are not unique across tables, and the schema cannot express a hierarchy-wide reference, so the union's keys must come from one source.
